vignette: He sits across from me in the third chair by the window, hands resting flat on his knees, palms down. At thirty-nine, he carries himself with the measured stillness of a man who spends his life navigating sudden shifts in pressure, though his breathing has settled into a shallow rhythm since the session began. He is Oceania by heritage, though his family scattered across the diaspora years ago, leaving him with a quiet sense of grounding he no longer quite accesses. His divorce is three years behind him, settled on paper but still echoing in the empty rooms of his city apartment. He flies wide-body jets across the Pacific, yet today he tells me he cannot listen to the cabin announcements without counting the syllables, waiting for the wrong word to drop. He describes the incident two years ago as if it is unfolding now. He stands off-duty at a regional terminal, waiting for a colleague, when a police radio crackles through a nearby officer's shoulder mic. A domestic call has escalated, a weapon appears, and then the shouts. He watches through the terminal glass as four officers move in. The first gunshot tears through the glass like paper. He remembers the sharp smell of cordite, the sudden vacuum of air, the way his own legs refuse to move while a woman three rows away drops her coffee cup. He stays in the waiting area for hours afterward, unable to speak, unable to leave, until a uniformed sergeant asks him to come down to the briefing room. He does. He sits through the debriefings, nodding when expected, while his skin burns and his vision narrows to the polished floor. The weeks that follow the incident settle into a heavy routine. He parks three blocks from work to avoid seeing emergency vehicles idling. At home, he stops watching the news after the first broadcast of the incident plays on a lobby screen; the repetition feels like another wound being picked. His ex-wife leaves him quietly, unable to navigate the wall of silence he has built around himself. He tells me he does not feel angry or sad anymore. He feels nothing but a low, persistent hum behind his ribs. When he sleeps, he wakes at 3:00 a.m. exactly, heart hammering, scanning the ceiling for shadows that mirror the angle of the gunman's stance. He keeps a locked drawer in his desk, not for use, but for the quiet certainty of its contents, a silent anchor to a reality he no longer trusts. Now, back in the cockpit, the discipline of the checklist has become both a lifeline and a cage. He runs through pre-flight inspections with mechanical precision, but his eyes linger on the emergency exits, mapping escape routes before the captain even boards. Radio static makes his shoulders seize. When the co-pilot jokes about a rough approach, he laughs too loudly, the sound brittle and foreign to his own ears. He has learned to breathe in the rhythm of the engines, to let the hum of the yoke ground him when the memories press against his sternum. He tells me in our session that he misses the sky, but not the ground beneath him anymore. He leaves the session when the clock ticks past the hour, straightening his jacket as if preparing for a takeoff that never comes, walking out into the afternoon light with his gaze fixed on the horizon, waiting for a horizon that feels dangerously close to breaking.
